segments.title: Approaching Fushimi-Momoyama Castle
segments.body: The visit begins with two travellers in Kyoto choosing the castle while the rest of their group visits a railway museum. The climb soon becomes the main historical observation: reaching Fushimi-Momoyama is tiring before any fortification comes into view. A joke about choosing somewhere else to conquer captures the deterrent effect of the hill. An attacker would spend energy simply reaching the defended ground. The castle's position makes the terrain part of its defence.

evidence.note: The speakers identify the castle, describe the hill climb, and frame the approach as discouraging to a would-be conqueror.

segments.summary: At Fushimi-Momoyama Castle in Kyoto, the visit begins with the climb and an immediate impression of how the uphill approach itself discourages an attacker.

segments.title: Verticality as the castle's first defense
segments.body: The castle's primary defence is jokingly named "verticality," a reference to the long climb and seemingly endless stairs. The discussion then compares the visitors' exertion with the burden on soldiers of the period. Attackers may have been fitter and more accustomed to the terrain, but armour and weapons would add weight and strain. They would arrive at the defended position tired and less able to move freely. The exchange gives a practical explanation of how elevation can increase a fortification's defensive value.

evidence.note: The speakers describe the endless stairs, name verticality as the primary defense, and compare themselves with armoured soldiers.

segments.summary: The steep stairs at Fushimi-Momoyama Castle prompt a practical reflection on how elevation, armour, weapons, and fatigue shape an assault.

segments.title: Comparing Fushimi-Momoyama Castle with Total War
segments.body: Fushimi-Momoyama Castle is compared directly with Japanese castles in Total War. Its visible resemblance answers blanket claims that the game's castles lack historical grounding. The point concerns appearance alone. The short clip does not test the game's map layouts, siege mechanics, or the accuracy of any specific digital model. It is a concise example of using a real site to assess historical visual design in a game.

evidence.note: At the castle, Dr. Clarke says it looks like the castles in Total War and uses the real site to challenge a blanket claim that those depictions are ahistorical.

segments.summary: Fushimi-Momoyama's resemblance to Japanese castles in Total War leads to a quick check of the game's visual claims against a real site.
